verdicts.evidence: The platform value is incorporated into platformKey, which the membership decision reads in the same function (s1, s2).
The six keys cover darwin, linux and win32 with both supported architectures and LE; membership takes the then side only for these platform values (f1:27, s2).
The condition reads process.platform, an operating system property (s1).
The os import resolves to the built-in os module, and arch() contributes to platformKey tested by the membership decision (f1:25, s3, s2).
Every supported OS has entries for arm64 and x64, with no other architecture entries in knownPackages (f1:27, s2).
The condition reads os.arch(), which supplies the machine architecture used to select the package (s3).
The built-in os module supplies endianness(), whose result contributes to the key read by the membership decision (f1:25, s4, s2).
All six supported keys end in LE, so reaching the membership then side requires LE byte order (f1:27, s4, s2).
Byte order from os.endianness() is an architecture property (s4).
The table contains the complete Cartesian product of the three claimed OS values and two architectures, exclusively with LE byte order; membership therefore requires all three conditions (f1:27, s2).
An unsupported key throws before package preparation, and rejection prevents the validation callback; a supported key enables the installation and validation paths (f1:44, f1:217, f1:246).
The successful membership branch proceeds on supported host platforms, while unsupported hosts throw; this is activation on supported targets (s2, f1:44).
The table maps host OS, architecture and byte order to platform-specific binary packages, and unsupported combinations throw (f1:27, f1:39).

The selector must return successfully before s5 runs, and s6 runs only after preparation resolves; its unsupported branch throws (f1:44, f1:217, f1:246). The cited calls resolve to their declared functions and reach the fetch, write, process, cleanup and validation sinks in the stated order (s8–s19)

The complete file has no exports or independent callers of the payload functions: preparation starts with the selector, and both validation calls are in its fulfillment callback (f1:216, f1:246). The recursive cleanup and redirect calls remain downstream of that same successful selector.

fetch reaches the imported https.get and buffers the response, while the other cited sinks resolve to fs.writeFileSync, fs.unlinkSync and child_process execution APIs (f1:54, f1:115, s10, s11, s14).
